strengths: Addresses a timely and important threat: training-time steganographic exfiltration in LLMs, extending TrojanStego.
Introduces a novel geometry-based approach using random hyperplane projections in embedding space for both secret encoding and vocabulary bucketing.
Formalizes payload recoverability along two complementary axes (bucket inference and secret recovery), providing a diagnostic framework that highlights limitations of prior work.
Broad empirical evaluation across three models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full and LoRA fine-tuning, two datasets (Wiki and TrojanStego), OOD prompt evaluation, and text quality metrics.
Demonstrates consistent exact match improvements over ASCII+Parity baseline, especially for LoRA and 70B (e.g., 9→19% +123% on Llama-70B), showing geometric bucketing helps learning.
Detection analysis via linear probes suggests fine-tuning leaves internal signatures, and the XOR masking control attempts to isolate internal traces from output decodability.
Includes an impact statement, honest limitations discussion, and a responsible disclosure plan.
weaknesses: The payload recoverability metric is not operational for a keyless defender: training classifiers to predict bits or secrets requires labeled bits/secrets, which the defender lacks under the stated threat model. Thus 'low recoverability' is not demonstrated for the intended adversary.

Detection via linear probes also requires supervised labels (bit values or secret embeddings) to train probes, so it is not a practical detection method for unknown malicious fine-tuning; the paper does not show an unsupervised or label-free detector.

The theoretical bounds (Thm 7.1, 7.2) rely on strong simplifying assumptions and are lower bounds, not upper bounds, so they do not establish that large payloads can be hidden within typical fine-tuning ranges. The perplexity bound uses a nonstandard evaluation (Q on P's top token) and only guarantees PPL ≥ ~2.

The XOR masking control is confounded by the secret being present in the prompt: probes may recover the secret from prompt representations rather than from a steganographic signature. Base model probes also show above-chance accuracy, and detection fails in many XOR cases (Table 3).
Attack exact match rates remain low (e.g., 19% on 70B, 26–43% on 8B LoRA), and no error-correcting code or robustness analysis is provided, limiting practical exfiltration.
The reported bucket recoverability for embedding bucketing (~0.6–0.7) is still far above chance, so the scheme is not 'unrecoverable'; the term 'low-recoverability' is relative and overstated.

Lack of comparison to benign fine-tuning for detection: the paper claims standard steganalysis is insufficient but does not empirically compare KL/perplexity shifts from stego fine-tuning to those from benign fine-tuning on the same data.
Reproducibility is limited: attack code is not released, and some details (hyperplane seed search, collision-free encoding, 70B training hardware) are missing.

Presentation issues: typos (e.g., 'Merit et al.' for Merity et al., 'Mistral AI team'), confusing proof notation (e.g., Eq. 6 duplicate t*), and some claims (e.g., '33% higher accuracy') are not clearly quantified.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: covert data exfiltration via fine-tuned LLMs in air-gapped/private deployments, with a clear training-time threat model.

Reasonable experimental breadth: three models (Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-3.3-70B), two prompt datasets (WikiText-103, TrojanStego-style), full vs LoRA fine-tuning, and an out-of-distribution prompt evaluation (Table 2).

Introduces a useful two-axis framing of payload recoverability (R_bucket, R_secret) and provides a control (secret-conditioned XOR masking, Section 7.4 / Appendix G) intended to decouple detection from output-side decoding.
Includes honest limitations discussion (Conclusion) and an impact statement with a stated responsible-disclosure plan for the attack code.
weaknesses: The recoverability metric is circular for the stated keyless defender. R_bucket = max_h Acc(h(O), b) and R_secret = max_h,g Acc(g(h(O)), S) both require labeled payloads (b or S) to train the classifiers (Appendix C: '80/20 split of steganographic outputs'). A defender who possesses b/S already has the payload, so the metric conflates 'detection/estimation' with 'recovery' and does not measure what a keyless analyst can actually do.

The detection method is likewise circular. The embedding-regression probe's target is constructed from the secret letters ('Concatenate input embeddings of 4 secret letters', Appendix F.4), so training the probe requires knowing the secret; the paper never explains how a keyless defender obtains labeled stego samples for the deployed model. Bit-classification probes are also redundant: if the defender 'knows the bucketing scheme' (Section 7.3), the bits are computable directly from the output tokens, so the probe adds no detection capability.

No benign-fine-tuning control. The base-vs-fine-tuned probe gap (e.g., ~60% -> 95-100% bit accuracy) could simply reflect that any fine-tuning increases attention to/representation of the in-prompt secret, rather than a stego-specific signature. Base models already reach ~60% bit accuracy, undermining the interpretation that probes recover 'the secret'.

Missing decisive baseline: keyed-random bucketing (a random secret seed applied to token IDs). Since both the proposed embedding-hyperplane scheme and any keyed scheme have unknown keys to the defender, the 'low recoverability' claim is largely trivial unless geometry is shown to outperform a keyed-random partition; that comparison is absent, so the claimed benefit of embedding geometry is not isolated from merely using a secret key.

Theoretical bounds are only loosely connected to the claims. Theorems 7.1/7.2 assume uniform bucket targets and specific distributions (p1=0.5, p2=0.3), yield expected/per-token quantities, and the assertion that the required KL/perplexity falls 'within typical fine-tuning ranges' is asserted rather than quantified or empirically validated against benign fine-tuning of the same models.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent. Absolute exact-match rates are low (e.g., 9->19%, 24->43%, 17->30%), several schemes underperform the baseline (e.g., E+E T on Ministral: -10%, A+E W on Ministral: -20%), and Table 1 highlights 'best Δ per column', which overstates the reliability of the improvements. The 'state-of-the-art recovery' claim is not supported at these absolute accuracy levels.

Confounded comparisons: the paper changes generation length (32 vs 128 tokens), datasets, LoRA rank (8 vs 128), epochs, and quantization simultaneously with the encoding/bucketing scheme, so improvements cannot be attributed to the geometric encoding.

Limited originality. Hyperplane-projection bucketing is adapted from watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023; Hou et al., 2024) and the detection uses standard linear probes (Alain & Bengio, 2016); the combination applied to TrojanStego is incremental, and the XOR/keystream construction is a routine keying idea.

Presentation and reporting issues: overlapping/hidden markers in Figure 2 ('markers are hidden under those of ASCII+Parity'), confusing table annotations (e.g., 'Best Δ per column: W / T'), missing error bars in some cells (Table 3), and abstract figures that do not exactly match the body (e.g., 17->30% labeled +78%; '+33%' used for different quantities).

Reproducibility is partial: detection code is promised but attack code is withheld, and key details of the recoverability classifiers and probe training are only lightly specified, limiting independent verification of the central claims.

strengths: The paper formalizes payload recoverability along two complementary axes, R_bucket and R_secret, using classifier accuracy, which is a useful diagnostic beyond standard distributional steganalysis.

It introduces embedding-space hyperplane-based encoding and bucketing schemes that are seed-dependent and, in several settings, improve exact-match attack success over the ASCII+Parity baseline while reducing classifier-based recoverability (e.g., Llama-8B LoRA 17→30%, Ministral-8B LoRA 24→43%, Llama-70B 9→19%).

The experimental scope is broad, covering multiple models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full and LoRA fine-tuning, Wiki and TrojanStego-style datasets, in-distribution and OOD prompt evaluations, and text-quality metrics.

The detection-side idea of using linear probes on later-layer activations is promising, and the reported bit-probe separation between fine-tuned and base models (e.g., ~95–100% vs ~60% final-layer accuracy) is striking.
The paper includes a dual-use impact statement and a responsible-disclosure plan, showing awareness of ethical risks.
The theoretical KL/perplexity bounds, despite limitations, provide a useful motivation for why output-level distributional steganalysis may be insufficient for fine-tuning-based covert channels.
weaknesses: The implementation and interpretation of payload recoverability are unclear and potentially inconsistent. R_bucket is defined via classifiers that require true bit labels, which a keyless defender does not have. As a supervised upper bound this can be conservative, but it is not clear how the classifiers are trained in practice. More importantly, for embedding-based bucketing the token-to-bucket assignment is a deterministic function of the token embedding, so a classifier with token IDs and labels should be able to memorize it almost perfectly; yet Figure 2 reports low R_bucket (~0.6). The paper does not explain this discrepancy, which undermines the central low-recoverability claim.

The detection evaluation lacks a benign fine-tuned baseline. All probe comparisons are between base models and steganographically fine-tuned models. Fine-tuning itself changes internal representations, and prompts include the secret in plaintext, so probes may be detecting generic fine-tuning effects or the presence of a prompt-borne secret rather than a steganographic channel. Without false-positive controls on benign fine-tuned models, the claimed 'actionable internal signatures' are not established.

The theoretical detection argument has technical problems. Theorem 7.2 assumes Q can assign probability mass to the base model's top token even when that token is outside the required bucket, which conflicts with the constrained generation used in the attack. There is also a mismatch between the theorem's PPL(Q) formulation and the empirical perplexity in Figure 4, which is computed as the base model's perplexity on fine-tuned outputs. The bounds are also very weak (e.g., KL ≈ 0.026 nats, PPL ≥ ≈2) and rely on strong assumptions, so they do not by themselves demonstrate that standard steganalysis is ineffective.

The attack results are modest and mixed in absolute terms: exact-match rates are often below 50%, some embedding-based methods underperform the ASCII+Parity baseline, and OOD generalization is poor (many 0–20% on new prompt styles). The abstract and introduction emphasize best-case relative gains, which overstates the practical strength of the channel.

The detection probes are not yet shown to be a practical detector. Bit detection succeeds in only three of eight XOR-masking scenarios, embedding recovery is less pronounced, and there is no ROC analysis, threshold selection, or calibration for deployment. The 'up to 33% higher accuracy' claim is relative and not consistently achieved across settings.

Reproducibility is only partial. Training details are provided, but attack code is withheld, and important experimental details (exact prompt templates, seeds, evaluation code for recoverability classifiers, and how labels are handled) are either incomplete or scattered. Several references and citations in the appendix are garbled, and the proofs contain notation errors (e.g., confused indices in the expected KL derivation).

Presentation is dense and sometimes confusing. Terminology such as 'exact secret recovery' is used for attack success rather than defender recovery, and several figures/tables would benefit from clearer captions and explanation, especially Figure 2 and the recoverability classifiers.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem: training-time steganographic exfiltration in LLMs, and it formalizes payload recoverability along two useful axes (tokens-to-buckets and buckets-to-secrets), making explicit that prior TrojanStego-style schemes are trivially recoverable.

The empirical evaluation is broad: Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, and Llama-70B under full and LoRA fine-tuning, Wiki/TrojanStego/mixed-motive datasets, out-of-distribution prompt tests, text-quality metrics, and capability benchmarks. The A+E scheme consistently improves exact-match accuracy over parity baselines in several settings.

The mechanistic detection study is interesting: linear probes on later-layer activations show a substantial gap between fine-tuned and base models, and the XOR-masking control attempts to isolate internal signatures from output-side decodability. This is a promising direction for defenses beyond standard steganalysis.

The paper includes a limitations section that discusses threat-model assumptions, symbolic-task degradation, hyperplane-search scaling, and output-only detection. It also includes a dual-use impact statement and responsible-disclosure plan.

The high-level argument that fine-tuning-induced distributional shifts can mask covert channels, and that defenses may need to inspect internal representations, is valuable even if the theoretical bounds require correction.
weaknesses: The theoretical bounds in Theorems 7.1 and 7.2 appear invalid for the actual constrained-generation attack. The KL proof minimizes KL subject only to q_t <= q_t* for all t != t*, which allows probability mass on tokens outside the required bucket. But the attack constrains generation to tokens in the required bucket, so Q(t)=0 outside that bucket. The derived bound is therefore for a weaker argmax-promotion problem, not the steganographic channel. Similarly, the perplexity proof allows Q(t1)=1/2 when t1 is not in the required bucket, which is infeasible under constrained support; the true perplexity can be much larger or infinite. Consequently, the central claim that large payloads can be hidden while keeping KL/perplexity within normal fine-tuning ranges is not established.

The recoverability metric assumes a defender with labeled secrets/bits to train classifiers. In the experiments, classifiers are trained on an 80/20 split of outputs with known secrets, making this a known-plaintext setting rather than a truly keyless one. The paper does not evaluate sample complexity, adaptive seed-recovery attacks, or stronger classifier families; thus the 'low-recoverability' claim is only relative to the tested XGBoost/MLP probes and finite data.

The detection method is not a standalone detector. The probes require ground-truth secrets or bit labels for training, and the experiments show that the secret is linearly decodable from hidden states rather than that an unknown steganographic fine-tune can be flagged without known secrets. The XOR control also shows weak bit detection in several scenarios (only 3 of 8 cases), and Ministral full fine-tuning remains hard to separate. Hidden-state access further limits applicability to white-box/open-weight settings.

The attack contribution is weaker than claimed: the embedding-based secret encoding (E+E) often underperforms ASCII+Embedding, and the best-performing scheme is ASCII+Embedding, meaning most gains come from the embedding-based bucketing alone. Exact-match rates remain low (e.g., 43%, 30%, 19% in key settings), and OOD generalization is poor in many configurations, limiting practical significance.

The paper has presentation issues that hinder assessment: dense and confusing tables (especially Table 1 with delta columns and hidden markers in Figure 2), some typos (e.g., 'Merit et al.' instead of Merity et al.), and the theoretical claims are not tightly linked to the empirical n=2 bucket setting. Attack code is not released, which reduces full reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important security problem: training-time steganographic exfiltration in LLMs, and proposes an embedding-geometry-based attack plus a mechanistic detection direction.
Introduces a useful conceptual decomposition of payload recoverability into bucket inference and secret recovery, which could help structure future work if properly operationalized.

Provides theoretical KL and perplexity lower bounds suggesting that output-level distributional steganalysis may have inherent limits, even if the bounds are not tightly connected to the empirical attack.
Conducts a broad empirical study across several models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full and LoRA fine-tuning, multiple datasets, and encoding/bucketing combinations.
The XOR-masking control is a creative attempt to isolate internal detection from output-side decodability.
Includes a limitations section and impact statement, and acknowledges dual-use risks with a responsible-disclosure plan for attack code.
weaknesses: The central 'low-recoverability' claim is not convincingly established. R_bucket and R_secret are defined as maximum classifier accuracy, but the experiments train supervised classifiers using ground-truth bit/secret labels. In a real keyless setting the defender lacks such labels; conversely, if labels are available, a linear classifier on full token embeddings could likely recover the hyperplane bucketing much better than the reported ~0.6 accuracy. The low recoverability may therefore be an artifact of PCA dimensionality reduction and limited classifier capacity rather than a fundamental property.

The security of the scheme relies entirely on a secret random seed, yet the paper uses a fixed seed (σ=42) in all experiments and provides no seed-space analysis, no seed-recovery evaluation, and no adaptive-attacker study. The claim that a keyless analyst must search a large space is asserted rather than quantified.

The detection claims lack critical controls. Linear probes are compared only between fine-tuned and base models, not against benign fine-tuned models. Since both base and fine-tuned models see the secret in the prompt, probe recovery may reflect general prompt information rather than a unique steganographic signature. No false-positive rate, threshold, or detection utility is established.

The theoretical bounds are not tied to the empirical attack. The KL/perplexity bounds analyze an optimal per-context distribution that promotes a target token to argmax, while the trained models' measured KL and perplexity (Figure 4) are far larger than the bounds. No benign fine-tuning baseline is provided, so the claim that distributional steganalysis is insufficient remains empirically unsupported.

Attack performance is modest: best exact match is 43% on Ministral LoRA and 19% on Llama-70B, meaning most secrets fail to be recovered. The abstract's relative improvements (+78%, +80%, +123%) can mislead readers about absolute reliability.

The strongest attack (ASCII+Embedding) uses ASCII secret encoding, not the proposed embedding-based secret encoding; Embedding+Embedding is often worse. This weakens the claim that replacing arbitrary mappings with embedding-space-derived ones improves both encoding and bucketing.

The detection method assumes access to hidden states and known secrets for probe training, and its extension to output-only or black-box settings is left entirely open. This limits practical significance.

Reproducibility is limited: attack code will not be released, and several critical details (seed handling, collision-free search, exact recoverability classifier training protocol) are insufficiently specified.

Presentation is dense and occasionally confusing: table abbreviations are hard to parse, notation is inconsistent (e.g., L_secret vs L_tx), and the abstract overstates the contribution by implying both encoding and bucketing are embedding-derived when the best results use ASCII encoding.

The paper does not adequately discuss or evaluate adaptive countermeasures, such as an adversary who knows the scheme family and attempts to recover the hyperplane partition from many unlabeled outputs or by exploiting the fixed seed.

strengths: The paper provides a clean and useful formalization of payload recoverability along two complementary axes (R_bucket for tokens->bits and R_secret for bits->secret), grounded in classifier-based steganalysis. This gives a principled way to compare schemes and convincingly demonstrates that prior work (TrojanStego's ASCII+parity) is trivially recoverable (100% on both axes).

The geometric attack idea—using seed-dependent random hyperplane projections in the token embedding space for both secret encoding and vocabulary bucketing—is novel, well-motivated, and intuitively explained. The argument that defining the channel in the model's learned geometry makes it easier to learn while harder to reverse-engineer without the seed is coherent and supported by the recoverability plots.

The empirical evaluation is broad: three models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full and LoRA fine-tuning, three data distributions (Wiki, TrojanStego, Mixed-motive), OOD prompt generalization, text-quality metrics, and capability benchmarks (MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag/WinoGrande). The mixed-motive regime and temperature/retokenization robustness analyses in the appendix add practical depth.

The mechanistic-interpretability detection angle is interesting and goes beyond standard distributional steganalysis. The XOR-masking control is a clever design that isolates internal signatures from output-decodable information, and the demonstration that the probe signal survives mixed-motive training and OOD prompts is a genuinely useful finding.

The theoretical bounds on KL divergence and perplexity (Theorems 7.1/7.2) provide a principled explanation for why output-level steganalysis is insufficient for fine-tuning-based attacks, and the proofs in Appendix B are reasonably complete and clear.

The paper is transparent about limitations (threat-model assumptions, symbolic-task degradation, hyperplane-search scaling, output-only detection) and includes a responsible dual-use statement with disclosure plans and detailed appendix hyperparameters, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The detection contribution is not evaluated as an actual detector. No decision threshold, ROC/AUC, or false-positive/false-negative analysis is provided; the claim rests on a gap in probe accuracy between fine-tuned and base models, while base-model probes already reach ~60% (above chance). It is unclear how a practitioner would set a detection criterion or quantify reliability, so the “detection” claim is more of an analysis than a usable defense.

The “low-recoverability” framing is somewhat overstated. Figure 2 shows R_bucket remains roughly 0.6–0.7 for embedding bucketing, well above the paper's own definition of unrecoverable (R_bucket ≈ 50%). The improvement is relative to the trivially recoverable baseline, not an absolute reduction to chance, so the central label should be tempered.

Absolute attack success rates remain modest (best exact match 43% for a 32-bit/4-letter secret), and several claimed improvements have overlapping error bars (e.g., E+E T on Ministral 38±6 vs A+P 24±2), so parts of the reported gains may be within noise and the practical viability of the channel is not fully established.

The recoverability metric assumes the defender can obtain labeled (token, bit) pairs to train the R_bucket classifiers; how such labels are acquired by a keyless defender in practice is not discussed, and the reported recoverability values may depend on this unstated assumption.

The geometric encoding of the secret (secret->bits) does not reduce R_secret (the authors acknowledge this), and ASCII+Embedding frequently outperforms Embedding+Embedding (e.g., Table 1). This undercuts the emphasis on the geometric encoder, making the encoding contribution largely incremental relative to the bucketing contribution.

Detection relies on white-box access to hidden states, restricting applicability to open-weight models; this is acknowledged but materially limits the reach of the defense claim. Additionally, several notation/reference inconsistencies (e.g., “Merit et al., 2016” vs Merity; “Tramèr et al., 2025” vs 2016; inconsistent L_secret/L_tx and R_bucket definitions mixing bits and buckets) reduce clarity.
